<reason>A genuinely close, high-quality debate. A framed the commons case vividly and asked sharp pressure questions, but B built the stronger path to victory: it neutralized A's central image by disclaiming fenced sand from the outset (Chicago's free lakefront, Central Park's free Great Lawn) while still defending the paid experiences the motion actually targets, turned the motion's own "broadly free" standard against A, and won the funding clash via the frequency/visibility asymmetry (a signed lease pays its full term; appropriations must win annually forever; quiet crew cuts vs visible ropes). A never answered B's streets-are-metered rebuttal, and A's closing contradicted A's own Rebuttal 2 on ticketed decks — "sells the view" became "never enclosure" — which B's closing directly exposed, collapsing A's claim that B had conceded the motion.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's closing reversal: when A declared "they have given the case away" for rejecting ticketed sand, B showed the motion opposes "paid private experiences" (rink, deck, wheel) that B defended all along — so A's mid-debate vendor-vs-gate line shrank the proposition's target to a fence nobody was defending. Combined with B4.4's "my model needs one victory and a filing cabinet," it gave B the decisive weighing edge.</best_rebuttal>
